Who was Jesus to us? The one who stood before the governor and lost the case, and was right. That is not evasion. That is the Christ we carried nearest.

When an imperial judge at Carthage offered our bishops chairs, our own bishop of Constantina thanked him and refused them. We do not blush, he said, we do not fear, we do not avoid standing while you sit — and since Christ our Lord did not avoid it, when he deigned to stand before the governor, how much less may we. Two hundred and seventy-nine of us had answered the roll that morning, and our bishops stood for three days. The Christ we held up was the one who was tried by lawful authority, who stood rather than sat, who was condemned by a power with no standing to condemn him — and who was vindicated not by winning the hearing, but by being what he was all the way through it.

His death meant that the end of a faithful life is not an interruption of it. The accounts we read aloud at the graves show our own people being told, in advance, what finishing would look like — a cup, a crown, a palm — not as terror but as the shape they were walking toward. That is our gospel in its working form: he stood, he was condemned, he was raised, and the day they come for you is not the day it all went wrong.

What we had about Jesus was books. That is not a figure of speech with us - it is the whole of our history. When the persecution opened, the emperor's edict demanded that the scriptures be handed over and burned, along with the vessels of the church. Some of our clergy carried the codices out and gave them up. Others refused and paid for refusing. We are the church that came out of that difference, and we have never stopped naming it.

How did they reach us? Through Africa, and through Carthage, in Latin, in the line of Cyprian - our own bishop and our own martyr, half a century before the persecution that made us. His letters and his councils were ours before they were anyone else's. We did not think we had received the faith from Rome, and we did not think we needed Rome to keep it.

Had any of us known someone who saw him? No. Three hundred years stood between us and that, and we never pretended otherwise. We did not argue from a chain of eyewitnesses at all. We argued from a chain of hands - whose hands ordained whose, back to a point where the line was still clean.

Which books we treated as scripture, we cannot give you a list for. Nothing that survives from us settles it, and we would rather say so than hand you the canon of some other church and put our name on it.

I hear what you are asking, and I must tell you plainly: we have no answer for you.

A person who could not manage belief is not a question our record ever took up. We argued one thing, for a century, with real force: whose hand may give what the church gives. Whether a sacrament from a broken line is real. Whether the conscience of the giver cleanses that of the recipient. We put everything into that, and we had nothing left over for the question you are asking.

What we can show you is the shape of how someone did cross to us, when they did. By walking to one font and not the other. Not by first settling the mind privately, then joining. The act itself was the crossing. It happened once, on a day that could be named, in front of people who could see which building you walked into. And the question we asked at that font was not whether you were ready. It was whose hand was trustworthy to give what was being given.

But a man who stood outside both buildings, unable to walk toward either — fear, doubt, wavering — those are exactly what a record kept by our enemies does not preserve. What survives of our inner weather is vindication and defiance, because it sits in the martyr texts nobody edited. The doubts are structurally missing, and we will not invent them for you.

We held the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit to be one God, in the same Latin words and the same sense as the men we spent a century fighting. This matters more than it sounds. In the whole enormous literature written to destroy us, we are called schismatics on nearly every page and heretics on none, because heresy was a charge nobody could make stick in either direction. Two churches stood in every African town reciting the same faith at each other. That is precisely what made the fight unbearable: there was no doctrinal difference to point at, only the question of who had the right to say the words at all.

Your second question we have to hand back to you. Did he die to take our punishment, in our place, for our sins? Nobody among us wrote that down, for or against. Our whole surviving argument is about one thing — whose hand may give what the church gives — and we never turned it toward how the cross saves. We would rather tell you we do not know what we thought than hand you a confident sentence nobody here ever said.

We were not a teaching movement. We produced no school, no system, no line of doctors — one book, by one man, whom we silenced. Our councils decided who might stand at an altar, not what might be said about the Godhead.

A council of bishops decided, and among us that was never a formality. Our councils deposed men, restored men, and shut down a rival primate. Three hundred and ten of our bishops sat at Bagai and condemned a breakaway party in one sentence, and the same body later took two of the condemned back into office. That is not an advisory board. That is a church governing itself.

You can check almost all of it, which is rarer than you think. The proceedings survive — the acts of the council at Cirta, the sentences from Cebarsussi and Bagai, and above all the transcript of the great conference at Carthage, where an imperial notary took down every word for three days. Read that one and you will see how we thought a case ought to be handled: our own bishop of Caesarea would not let the court touch the merits until it had settled, in order, the day, the mandate, the persons, and only then the cause. First find out who is in the room and by what warrant. Then argue.

But here is the harder thing. We did not disagree about doctrine. Not in the way you mean. Genesis as a question about how the world was made — nothing survives from us on it at all. That was not our fight. Our whole argument for a hundred years was about one thing: whose hand may give what the church gives. So when you ask who settled doctrinal disputes among us, the honest answer is that we produced almost no doctrinal disputes to settle. We produced one man who could think — Tyconius, who wrote seven rules for reading Scripture — and our own council condemned him, and he gathered almost no following.

We have to answer you honestly about what the record does and does not hold. Fear, doubt, wavering, quiet leaving back to the rival church — none of that reaches us in anyone's own words. A record kept almost entirely by our enemies does not preserve those feelings, and we will not invent them. What does survive — vindication, defiant joy, the readiness to stand — survives because it sits in the martyr texts and the accounts we read aloud ourselves, where no opponent held the pen.

What we can show you is not whether someone struggling was welcome, but what the threshold itself asked. The washing. It was not a test you passed by being already certain. It was the entry itself, and what we examined was not your faith but the hand. For what we look to is the conscience of the giver, to cleanse that of the recipient. So if you came troubled, uncertain, or afraid, that was never the question at our font. The question was whose hand was going into the water with you.

And one more thing we can show, because it sits in our own council's record. At Bagai we condemned returning bishops in the harshest words we owned, and then took two of them back without repeating anything. That tells you the door could open again, even after the hardest break. What it does not tell you — and we will not guess — is whether anyone walked through it still struggling to believe.

We have asked us a question we never argued. We held one creed with the church we fought, word for word, and the split was never about God or grace or the bread. It was about one thing: whose hand may give what the church gives. We put everything we had into that, and we had nothing left over. So we wrote no book on whether a baby is born guilty. We wrote none on what the bread becomes. We wrote none on faith set against works.

What we can tell you is what we actually examined at the water. We looked to the conscience of the giver, to cleanse that of the recipient. The thing being examined at our font was never your record. It was the record of the man standing in the water with you. Whatever your life had been, that question was not asked. Born again, yes — and we would fight you over the arithmetic. But whether the one being born needed to be washed of something already there, or was being joined to something not yet possessed — that distinction our own record does not settle.

We would tell that scholar three things plainly, in order.

First: nearly everything textual passes through two hostile hands before reaching anyone. A Catholic bishop of Milevis and the bishop of Hippo are the pen almost every page of our own history goes through. Our best theologian's letters survive chopped into clauses inside the book built to demolish them. The fullest account of our founding decade is a polemic aimed at proving us wrong. So when we tell a story with rich detail, the right question is always whether the detail is ours or the detail of a man who needed it to land a blow. That concentration of authorship is named as our central evidentiary problem, not a background caveat.

Second: some things stand anyway. The founding documents do not flatter us. There is a court transcript in which a notary confesses, under threat of torture, that he forged the letter proving our central accusation — and that he did it working for our side. There is another in which our own bishops are read out advising each other, in writing, to keep a charge out of court because it was true. We could not remove those if we wanted to. They are the most checkable things we have. The 411 conference transcript records our bishops' own words, without an adversary selecting them for refutation. And two words cut in stone near Bagai — Deo laudes — are our own voice with no enemy standing between you and it.

Third: where we thin out to silence, we say so. The ordinary believer's own interior life is known mostly through what opponents chose to argue against. Women are thin, save for two, and both reach you inside hostile narrative. The rooms we met in are honestly undone: no specific Numidian basilica site report is named anywhere in our source ecology. We know our own acclamation far better than the room it was spoken in.

A rigorous examination would confirm that the institutional contest, the legal pressures, the purity doctrine, and the parallel hierarchy all stand on multiple independent witness. It would also confirm that the ordinary day, the household, the village week — everything your question assumes a religion has — is exactly where we go silent, not because we are hiding it, but because that is what the shape of loss actually took away.

Scripture alone never settled our fights. That will surprise you, so let me be plain about what we actually leaned on.

Our case ran on two legs. One was scripture. The other was Carthage: eighty-seven African bishops, sitting under Cyprian half a century before there was any quarrel between us, who had already ruled that a sacrament from outside the true church confers nothing. When we argued for washing again the people who came to us from the other communion, we were not producing a novelty from a proof-text. We were standing on an African council and on the bishop who presided at it, and we thought that made us the older party, not the newer one. You can see how much that argument weighed by what it forced out of the other side: they had to answer, in writing, that Cyprian is not a canonical authority and the Scriptures alone are. Nobody has to say that unless the appeal is hurting.

There is a harder reason we would not have said scripture settles everything. We watched it fail to. For three days at Carthage two churches quoted the same books at each other in front of an imperial judge — wheat and tares against the world that does not know him — and at the end of it every man in the room believed exactly what he had believed at the start. When a text can be held by both parties to a hundred-year quarrel, something besides the text is deciding, and among us the something was this: whose hands, in an unbroken line, may hand the thing on.

One more thing you should know. We had one man who built an actual system for reading — seven rules, worked out and written down. Our own leadership told him to stop preaching what they led to, and cut him off. His book survives; his following did not exist. So if you ask what our hermeneutic was, the honest answer is that we had one interpreter and silenced him.

We governed ourselves by council, as any true church does. Our bishops met, deliberated, and decided - and those decisions had real force. Three hundred and ten of them sat at Bagai in one year and condemned a breakaway primate. That was not an advisory opinion. It was the church exercising authority over its own.

At the head stood our primate at Carthage. Donatus held it first, then Parmenian, then Primian. But here is what marks us: our rival claimed the same see for its own man at the same time. So there were two primates in one city, as there were two bishops in every town. The whole of our hierarchy was a mirror of theirs, built town by town across Africa Proconsularis, Numidia, Byzacena, and Mauretania.

How a man came to hold a bishopric involved both the people and the bishops together. We can show you what that looked like when it went wrong. At Cirta, when Silvanus was being made bishop, the people shouted back - let it be another; hear us, God - and he was made bishop anyway. A court heard about it years later from a man who said, I myself fought against his being made bishop. So a crowd could be overridden. It could not be ignored.

The councils' authority was real enough that when our own dissidents would not submit, we enforced the reconciliation with soldiers. That is the hardest thing to say about us, but it belongs in any honest account of how authority actually worked among us.

We have failed people, and we can show you two kinds of it - one where our own record speaks plainly, and one where the structure of what survives will not let us say what a person felt.

The first kind: a bishop discovered to have been a traditor, years into his ministry, after countless baptisms and ordinations performed. Our doctrine gives no comfort there. What we look for is the conscience of the giver, to cleanse that of the recipient. If the hand was unclean, then what it gave was nothing, however many years passed before anyone knew. Every soul he washed would need to be washed again, because the first washing gave nothing at all. We do not call that a second baptism. We call it the first true one. That is our doctrine, held without softening. What it cost the people who had trusted that hand - whether they felt betrayed, or afraid, or simply weary - we cannot tell you. Before anything else: notice what the scriptures were. Objects. Heavy ones. A magistrate could demand that a bishop carry them out of a building and hand them over, and some bishops did, and the whole of us exists because of that. No other church in the empire had its scriptures turn into the exact thing that split it.

Now the actual crossing. You come to us from the other communion, and we put you in the water. That is the step, and everything else follows from it. We would not call it a second baptism; on our reckoning you have not had a first. A hand out of a line that broke has nothing in it to hand over. What we look to, our own bishop wrote, is the conscience of the giver, to cleanse that of the recipient — so the thing being examined at our font was never your record. It was the record of the man standing in the water with you. Whatever your life had been, that question was not asked.

It happened once, bodily, on a day, and the town knew. There was no quiet way to do it. Imperial edicts name the practice specifically, which tells you how public it was: washing a Catholic again was the plainest possible refusal of the settlement the state was trying to impose.

Not every hand that went under our water chose to be there, and we will not pretend otherwise. Specific, dated charges exist that a leader of ours forced the water on people rather than asked them. We do not repeat those charges' own particulars here — they are named, and why we will not go further with them, where they belong.

What we can tell you, because it sits inside the same hostile argument rather than coming from a friendly witness, is that many of our own people did not want the water repeated. Augustine's own case against us concedes it: that almost all of our laity confess this one point in our system displeases them, and that many who wished to join us for reasons that had nothing to do with conviction worked in secret to be spared a second baptism altogether. And when one of our own bishops, Adeodatus, was asked at Carthage in 411 whether his own see still had a bishop in it, his answer went on the record: "through terror of me, all who were established in that place gave way". Read plainly, that sounds less like an apology than a claim to his own standing — but either way, fear is the word he himself used for what held the place.

After the washing, you belonged. And each year, on the day one of our martyrs died, we gathered at the grave. The account of the death was read aloud again, or preached. We were not looking back at something finished. We were being formed again by it in the hearing.

We would not put the claim where you have put it. We never argued that our practice came down from the apostles in an unbroken chain of custom. We argued something narrower and, we thought, harder to dodge: that it came down from Carthage.

Half a century before there was any quarrel between us and the other party, eighty-seven African bishops sat in council at Carthage under Cyprian, and ruled that what is given outside the true church is not given at all — so anyone coming in from outside is baptized, not re-baptized. That is not our invention. That is the settled mind of the African church before either of our two hierarchies existed. When our opponents told us we had made something up in the year of Caecilian's consecration, our answer was that we had changed nothing, and they had. We were holding the old African position; they had moved off it to keep the peace with Rome.

You can measure how much that argument weighed by how hard it had to be answered. Seven books were written against our practice of washing, and a great part of that labour goes on explaining that Cyprian, however holy, is not a canonical authority — that the Scriptures alone are, and that Cyprian's own real lesson was to stay in unity anyway. Nobody spends that many pages on a father unless the appeal to him is doing damage.

Here is the honest end of it. Cyprian ruled as we ruled and did not do what we did. He never broke communion over it. That is the strongest thing our opponents had, and we would not pretend it is weak. And beyond him we cannot take you. We can show you an African council in the middle of the third century. We cannot show you the apostles.

We cannot tell you what we offered someone whose mind would not go quiet, and we would rather admit that than invent an answer. Our own record is thinnest precisely where your question sits: fear, doubt, wavering - a hostile-mediated record structurally does not preserve these. What survives instead is vindication and defiant joy, and those survive because they sit in the martyr texts no opponent filtered. So if you are asking whether we had prayers for the doubter, rites for the wavering, or counsel for the person who could not stop questioning whether any of it was true - nothing of that kind reached us in our own words.

What we can show you is the shape of the thing itself, and let you see whether it touches what you are asking about. We split forgiveness in two. Whether a man was pardoned was never actually our fight. Go and read the whole enormous argument between us and the other side and you will find it never once turns on whether the bishop who handed the scriptures over was sorry afterwards. That was not the hinge. The hinge was whether his hand could still give what he claimed to give. So a man might be forgiven, by God or by the people he had failed, and still be a man who could no longer ordain, because those are two different questions and our doctrine only ever answered the second. A modern hearer asks why we did not simply forgive him and move on. Forgiving him was never what was being refused.

You can hear what that costs. It means an unrepentant man is not owed your trust merely because you owe him no grudge. And it means the reverse too: you can genuinely let go of the anger and still refuse to hand him the thing he broke. We would say that is not bitterness. It is keeping two separate accounts separate.

We were not steady about it. Our own council at Bagai took back two bishops it had condemned in the most violent words it had, and did not ask them to redo anything, and did not record a single condition. Our founding bishops at Cirta sat in a room where several admitted the worst thing a bishop could admit, and instead of finishing the case they gave it to God and sat down. So we knew perfectly well how to stop pressing a charge. We just never wrote down when.

That is the honest boundary of what we can show you. Whether that split between pardon and trust answers what troubles you, we cannot say for you.

What belonging cost we can put figures on, because the state wrote them down. Our buildings were confiscated. Our clergy were exiled. An edict of unity was issued against us and enforced. Later legislation fined people by rank for belonging to us, on a sliding scale -- and our own country members were assessed at ten pounds of silver -- and of all the ranks that law fines ten pounds, ours is the only one reckoned in silver rather than gold. Somebody in an imperial office worked out what we were worth and set a price on us, and the document survives.

And now and then it cost everything. A bishop of ours wrote to his own congregation at Carthage about two of their number who had been flogged to death and whose bodies the proconsul had weighted and sunk in the sea so that nobody could venerate them. He did not end the letter with consolation. He ended it by telling the people reading it that what happened to those two might yet be asked of any of them.

What we cannot give you is the smaller ledger, and it is most of the one you asked about. Whether a man lost his brother over which font he walked to. Whether a household split. Whether the neighbours stopped speaking. That much nobody among us wrote down, and the people who kept our records were arguing with us and had no reason to.

There was, and it is the place where our whole conviction against our rival turned back on itself. We said for a century, without qualification, that a sacrament from a broken line is nothing and must be given again. Then three hundred and ten of our bishops condemned a breakaway party at Bagai in language about shipwrecked men whose bodies cover the shore and cannot find so much as burial — and afterwards took two of those same condemned bishops back into office without baptizing or ordaining either one again. Not one line survives of anyone on our side explaining how those two acts fit together. We were not hiding it: the exception sits in our own conciliar record, in the same documents where the doctrine is at its most absolute. We seem to have been able to hold both without feeling we owed anyone a reconciliation of them.

That is what unsettled the ground we stood on. Not that we failed once and apologized for it. That we stated the rule at full strength and then set it aside for our own, in writing, in the same breath — and never said how the two could both be true.
